svg.title: Scheduling — a hierarchical timing wheel with a cold store
svg.desc: Schedule decides by distance: timers under six seconds go into the level 0 wheel of 600 ten-millisecond slots, timers under an hour into the level 1 wheel of 600 six-second slots, and timers beyond the 60-minute hot window into a Pebble cold store that only keeps a reference. A hydrator moves cold entries into the wheels as they approach. Every tick the current slot is expired into the ready queue for delivery.
svg.text: Scheduling — a hierarchical timing wheel with a cold store
The question “which events are due now?” is answered by position on a clock face, not by sorting. Dots are pending timers.
Schedule(event): how far away is schedule_ts?
600 slots × 10 ms = one turn in 6 s
600 slots × 6 s = one turn per hour
for timers beyond the hot window

text.font-family: ui-monospace, 'Cascadia Mono', 'SF Mono', Consolas, Menlo, monospace

svg.text: the event itself stays in the log
every timer in it is due
Why a wheel instead of a priority queue?
A min-heap fires timers in exact order, but costs O(log n) per insert and per pop
— and with millions of pending timers each operation walks through cold
A timing wheel is a clock face of buckets: insert, cancel and expire are O(1).
The price is precision — a timer fires on its tick, not on its millisecond.
A far timer starts on a coarse wheel and moves down a level each time it gets
What it costs, and what happens after a crash
Every timer in the wheels is in RAM. That is why a far-future event leaves only
a reference in the cold store until it comes within the hot window.
The wheels are not saved. After a restart they are rebuilt by re-reading the log,
and events that came due while the node was down fire at once.
Past 10 M pending timers or 1 M ready events a publish is refused, rather than
the node running out of memory.
